# Results — Study 414 (Falling Wedge)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a falling
wedge (two downward-converging trendlines) is bullish: it breaks upward and runs** — tested with
the closest **mechanical** definition of the figure on daily OHLC: a run of *descending* swing
highs fit by a line, the intervening swing lows fit by a second line, **both slopes negative**, the
**upper line steeper** than the lower (the highs fall faster), the band **narrowing** toward an
apex, and a confirmed close above the extrapolated upper line — across **SPY + 29 US large-caps**.
We measure the forward return after each confirmed breakout as an **excess over each name's own
base rate** (does the figure beat buy-and-hold for that name?), with a one-sample/HAC *t*, a
**same-tape label-shuffle placebo**, a **down-break symmetry** myth-check, and a synthetic positive
control. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every
number.*

> **Chart figures are partly subjective.** The falling wedge is in the eye of the beholder. We do
> **not** claim to capture every wedge a human would draw — we test one transparent, reproducible
> mechanical definition and say so. A different rule set would find a different (overlapping) event
> set; the qualitative verdict is what travels.

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily **auto-adjusted** (split + dividend) OHLC — 30 long-listed US large-caps incl. SPY (public, no key) |
| As-of | **2026-05-31** (last full bar **2026-05-29**; no partial month) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**21.4** years; 5,385 daily bars) |
| Fingerprint | `eeb1719704c4` (sha1[:12] of the close panel) |
| Detector | descending swing-high line + swing-low line, **both slopes negative**, upper steeper, band narrows ≥25%, first close clearing the extrapolated upper line |
| Events | **219** confirmed falling-wedge **up**-breaks (SPY alone: **2**); **122** down-breaks (myth check) |
| Timing / costs | enter the close **1 day after** the breakout (no look-ahead); hold 5/10/20/40 days; **5 bps** one-way × 2 = 10 bps round trip |

> **Survivorship (named on the Signal axis).** The basket is 30 names *still trading* in 2026. A
> fixed surviving-names panel cannot include firms that delisted after a failed wedge break, which
> tilts post-breakout forward returns mildly **up** — i.e. the bias works *for* the figure, and it
> still doesn't certify. Total-return adjusted closes (we label them as such).

## The signal — forward return after a confirmed up-break, EXCESS over the base rate

The excess subtracts each name's own unconditional mean forward return, so the test is **"does the
figure beat buy-and-hold for that name?"** — not "is the market up." The **placebo p** is the share
of 5,000 draws of *random entry dates on the same tape* (same count) whose excess **beats** the
observed one — the honest control for the tape's own up-drift.

| horizon | n events | excess mean | raw mean | win-rate | one-sample *t* | HAC *t* | placebo *p* | net of costs |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 219 | −0.58% | −0.29% | 41% | **−2.57** | **−2.57** | 0.69 | −0.68% |
| 10-day | 219 | +0.28% | +0.84% | 55% | +0.72 | +0.82 | 0.44 | +0.18% |
| 20-day | 219 | +1.26% | +2.40% | 59% | **+2.19** | **+2.26** | 0.30 | +1.16% |
| 40-day | 216 | +1.80% | +4.03% | 60% | **+2.47** | **+2.73** | 0.29 | +1.70% |

Read it carefully — this is the whole study. Two things jump out. First, at the horizon a trader
would actually act on — the **breakout day** — the excess is **negative** (5-day −0.58%, *t* =
−2.57): the "buy the upside break" rule buys a *local high* right after a fall and gives some of it
straight back. Second, the longer-horizon excess does clear the desk's **t ≥ 2** bar at 20/40 days
(+1.26% / +1.80%, *t* ≈ 2.2–2.5) — taken alone that reads `REAL`. But the same-tape **placebo p
stays ~0.29**: a random set of entry dates on the same drifting names beats the breakout about
**three times in ten**. The *t*-against-zero is fooled because the breakout *selects post-selloff
dates on names that then keep grinding up* (the basket's own up-drift / mean-reversion-into-trend);
the placebo inherits that drift, the naive *t* does not. The number is real; its **attribution to
the wedge** is what's in doubt.

## Costs — they barely matter, because there's no placebo-clean edge to tax

A round trip is **5 bps one-way × 2 = 10 bps**. Net columns above. There is nothing to erode: the
gross excess is already inside the placebo cloud at every horizon, so costs are a footnote, not the
killer.

## Myth check — does it break UP specifically? (the symmetry test)

The cleanest within-study control. Run the **identical** detector but require a break *below* the
lower (support) line — the "bearish" resolution a chartist would call a *failed* wedge. If the
figure genuinely chooses an upward direction, the down-break excess should be **negative**, well
under the up-break.

| horizon | n | down-break excess | raw | win-rate | one-sample *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 122 | −0.40% | −0.12% | 45% | −0.91 | 0.61 |
| 10-day | 122 | +0.11% | +0.67% | 47% | +0.20 | 0.49 |
| 20-day | 121 | +1.80% | +2.91% | 51% | +2.00 | 0.28 |
| 40-day | 120 | +3.79% | +5.96% | 60% | +2.97 | 0.20 |

The down-break — the resolution a chartist would call **bearish** — *also* drifts **up** at 20–40
days (+1.80% / +3.79%, *t* = 2.00 / 2.97), and at 40 days it **beats** the up-break. A figure that
truly *chose* a direction could not have its two resolutions drift the same way (indeed the wrong
one harder). The post-figure return is a property of the **names** (down-then-up mean reversion),
not the **break direction**. "It breaks upward, specifically" is the part that's busted.

## Robustness — strictness moves the *t*, not the placebo

| narrowing / breakout buffer | n events | excess (20d) | one-sample *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| narrow ≥35% / buf 0.5% (strict) | 166 | +1.14% | +1.76 | 0.34 |
| **narrow ≥25% (headline)** | **219** | **+1.26%** | **+2.19** | **0.30** |
| narrow ≥15% (loose) | 264 | +1.41% | +2.73 | 0.26 |

The naive *t* swings with the sample (more events on a drifting tape → higher *t*), but the
**placebo p stays ~0.26–0.34 everywhere** — no setting pulls it under the 5% bar. That invariance
is the signature of a tape artefact: you can tune the *t*, you can't tune away the fact that random
dates do nearly as well.

## Myth check — does it beat SPY buy-and-hold? (the README hook)

The hook asks specifically about **SPY**. The detector finds only **2** clean falling wedges on the
SPY tape in 21 years — far too few to certify anything, and what little there is points *down* at
short horizons:

| horizon | n | excess vs SPY hold | raw | one-sample *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 2 | −3.30% | −3.06% | −0.97 | 0.97 |
| 10-day | 2 | −4.09% | −3.62% | −0.69 | 0.95 |
| 20-day | 2 | −5.67% | −4.73% | −1.14 | 0.96 |
| 40-day | 2 | +0.07% | +1.92% | +0.05 | 0.55 |

With *n* = 2 nothing is certifiable, and the broad-basket symmetry test already showed the breakout
direction is uninformative. The figure does **not** demonstrably beat SPY buy-and-hold.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful (and the placebo is the right arbiter)

On a deterministic panel where we **plant** clean falling wedges and a *known* post-breakout drift,
the detector + inference behave exactly as they must:

| planted edge | planted | detected | n | excess (20d) | one-sample *t* | placebo *p* | win-rate |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no edge) | 160 | 137 | 135 | −1.44% | −3.93 | 0.885 | 53% |
| **+0.40** (large planted drift) | 160 | 181 | 179 | +3.68% | **+4.36** | **0.087** | 33% |

With **no** planted continuation the detector finds **no positive edge** (excess −1.44%, the
breakout buys the snap-back high) and the **placebo does not reject** (p = 0.885). Plant a real
+40% post-breakout continuation and the mean **flips strongly positive** (+3.68%, *t* = 4.36) and
the placebo collapses toward significance (p = 0.087, and p ≈ 0.06 at a +60% plant). The engine
*can* bank a true continuation when one exists; the real tape simply doesn't have one once the
placebo speaks. This is precisely why we trust the placebo over the *t*.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The up-break excess-over-base-rate clears a naive bar at the slow horizons
  (**+1.26% at 20 days, one-sample t = 2.19, HAC t = 2.26**; +1.80% at 40 days, *t* = 2.47), but
  the same-tape **placebo p = 0.30** (luck wins ~3-in-10), the strictness sweep keeps *p* at
  ~0.26–0.34, and a **zero-edge synthetic control finds no positive edge at placebo p = 0.885**.
  The number is real; its attribution to the figure is not. **WEAK, not REAL** — the *t* clears 2
  only against a drifting-tape null the placebo corrects, and at the **breakout day itself the
  excess is negative** (5-day *t* = −2.57). Survivorship tilts the test *for* the figure and it
  still fails.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** What you'd be "trading" is the names' own down-then-up mean reversion —
  exactly what random dates capture. The breakout-day rule actually **loses** at 5 days; the
  SPY-only version rests on **2** events; costs are a footnote because there's no placebo-clean edge
  to tax. Nothing to deploy.
- **"Bullish — breaks up specifically"? — BUSTED.** The pattern's entire premise is a bullish
  *direction*, and the direction carries **no** information: the **down**-break of the identical
  figure also drifts up (+1.80% / +3.79% at 20/40 days, *t* = 2.00 / 2.97), beating the up-break at
  40 days. Break up or break down, the stock drifts up the same. The falling wedge is a
  mean-reversion tell dressed as a directional breakout signal.
